> For my first PCB project, I wanted to build something I could actually use at my computer every single day, so I designed a custom 3-key macro pad. It plugs in via USB and lets me hit physical mechanical switches to trigger shortcuts like copying, pasting, or muting myself on Discord. Instead of just using basic parts like my last three prototypes, this board steps things up by using an RP2040 microcontroller to handle the USB data lines and custom programming. The coolest part of the hardware design was routing the differential pairs for the USB-C port and creating the exact footprint cutouts for hot-swap mechanical keyboard switches. I also added a customizable RGB LED under each key just to give it a clean desktop aesthetic. It’s the perfect mix of hardware layout and coding!

## Design

### 2026-10-10 – Spent 10h hours obviously with a lot of brakes, locked into the design zone this week! Worked through the PCB routing, polished the hardware features, and got the 3d and code for the designed pcb. It'

**7h**

Spent 10h hours obviously with a lot of brakes, locked into the design zone this week! Worked through the PCB routing, polished the hardware features, and got the 3d and code for the designed pcb. It's super rewarding to watch it all come together.

Over the course of this deep-work session, I tackled the entire hardware and software pipeline. I finalized the electronic schematic and PCB layout in KiCad, integrating a Seeed XIAO RP2040 microcontroller to handle custom USB data lines and programming. Then it took me an hour deciding which is the smallest best microcontroller, as there were so many options. Then a few hours designing the gesture contols, it was prety hard to be honest, then i speant around 1.5 hours testing it on my Raspberry pi 5

![Screenshot 2026-10-10 at 2.04.56 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/EG1Tvn5mN8w3iHKu8EvhW1MqVtqDxkYt/d4db9501ea9d8bbbd9edf9eec074c7e58b0f91ae1890a0fcce3830ac7f30994f.png)

The design features a robust matrix of 6 MX-style mechanical switches paired with 1N4148 diodes, an EC11 rotary encoder for volume control or scrolling, a 0.91-inch OLED display for real-time telemetry, and a chain of 14 SK6812 MINI-E addressable LEDs providing vibrant RGB underglow. Beyond the physical circuit board, I programmed unique software workflows: a dedicated key mapping shortcut tool that lets users customize button commands on the fly, and an integrated AI webcam gesture-control feature that enables hands-free device navigation. Pushing through hours of detailed routing, soldering prep, and firmware logic resulted in a fully functional, desktop-ready input device that bridges hardware engineering with practical utility.
